## Dataset: Dataset Article &quot;Species composition shapes canopy microclimate and foliar traits without modifying photosynthetic thermal acclimation in a beech-oak ecotone&quot;, Deluigi et al.

&#42;&#42;Article: &quot;Species Species composition shapes canopy microclimate and foliar traits without modifying photosynthetic thermal acclimation in a beech-oak ecotone&quot;&#42;&#42;<br>Authors: &#42;&#42;Janisse Deluigi&#42;&#42;, Charlotte Grossiord, Alvaro Poretti, Lorenz Walthert, Christoph Bachofen<br>The study was conducted along a south-exposed elevational gradient ranging from 770 to 860 m a.s.l. in a central alpine valley &#40;46°10&#96;14&#96;&#96;N, 7°10&#96;01&#96;&#96;E, Saillon, Switzerland&#41;. Along the elevational gradient, we selected three forest stands characterized by high coverage of mature European beech &#40;Fagus sylvatica L.&#41; and downy oak &#40;Quercus pubescens Willd.&#41; trees, with are naturally distributed in three species combinations: one pure beech stand &#40;i.e., at least 80% of the basal area&#41; at 860 m a.s.l. , one mixed beech-oak stand &#40;i.e., similar relative abundances of the two species – at least 40% of the basal area each – and minimal presence of other tree species&#41; at 785 m a.s.l., and one pure oak stand &#40;i.e., at least 80% of the basal area&#41; at 770 m a.s.l. An additional forest clearing of around 0.04 ha next to the pure oak stand was selected as reference for conditions outside the forest  &#40;i.e., clearing or gap&#41;. At each forest stand, we selected five healthy, mature, overstory trees per tree species, resulting in a total of 20 individuals &#40;5 individuals x 2 species x 2 mixture combinations, i.e., mixed vs. pure forest stand&#41;. <br>&#42;&#42;Dataset 1: Climatic conditions at the study sites&#42;&#42;<br>In 2023 and 2024 we monitored climatic conditions at each forest stand and in the clearing using climatic stations with air temperature, relative humidity and radiation sensors installed at 1.8 m height in a central position relative to the selected trees for each site. The meteo station in the clearing site had additionally a rain gauge and wind sensor. <br>&#42;&#42;Dataset 2: Tree and canopy sizes&#42;&#42;<br>Once in 2023 we measured tree height and diameter at breast height of all selected trees using a vertex hypsometer and a caliper. In August 2023 and 2024 we estimated canopy size measuring the height at which canopy starts &#40;CS&#41;, canopy depth &#40;= tree height - CS&#41; and maximum canopy radius as the average of two orthogonal measurements &#40;south and east direction&#41; using a vertex hypsometer. We also estimated canopy total leaf area using species- and site-specific allometric equations from collected branches upscaled to the tree level.<br>&#42;&#42;Dataset 3: Microclimatic conditions measured in tree canopies&#42;&#42;<br>We monitored canopy microclimatic conditions in 2023 and 2024 attaching one air temperature and air humidity sensor &#40;HOBO&#41; on one branch at the top and one branch at the bottom of the south-exposed side of the canopy for each selected tree in June 2023.<br>&#42;&#42;Dataset 4: Physiological traits&#42;&#42;<br>During three field campaigns &#40;June, August, September&#41; per year &#40;2023, 2024&#41; we measured temperature response curves of leaf net photosynthesis and dark respiration. As in-situ measurements were not possible, tree-climbers collected one representative branch at the top and the bottom of the canopy from each selected tree at each site. Estimates of the thermal optimum of photosynthesis &#40;Topt&#41;, photosynthetic rate at Topt &#40;Aopt&#41;, respiration rate at a standard temperature of 25°C &#40;R25&#41; and thermal sensitivity of respiration &#40;Q10&#41; were extracted from the temperature response curves of photosynthesis and respiration, respectively. <br>Leaf water potentials at predawn and midday, as well as leaf chlorophyll content, were also measured on the same day for each selected tree at each site. <br>&#42;&#42;Dataset 5: Physiological traits - specific leaf area and leaf size&#42;&#42;<br>In August 2023 and 2024 we collected a random subset of 10 representative fully developed leaves of different sizes from a representative branch harvested at the top and bottom of the canopy of each selected tree to estimate the specific leaf area &#40;SLA&#41; and leaf size &#40;average of the 10 leaves&#41;.<br>&#42;&#42;Dataset 6: Soil water potentials&#42;&#42;<br>Hourly soil water potentials and soil temperature were recorded during the two years of measurements &#40;2023, 2024&#41; at each forest site at different soil depths: 20 cm, 80 cm, 140 cm and 200 cm.

## Load packages

This template targets tidyverse (2.x) and skimr (2.x) with R 4.1 or newer for the native `|>` pipe; package versions are not pinned. Install missing packages once with `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "skimr"))`.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

USER_AGENT <- "OpendataSwiss-StarterCode-R/1.0"
HTTP_TIMEOUT <- 30

get_dataset <- function(url, delim = NULL, drop_empty_unnamed = TRUE, ...) {
  if (grepl("^https?://", url)) {
    local_file <- tempfile()
    on.exit(unlink(local_file), add = TRUE)
    old_options <- options(timeout = HTTP_TIMEOUT)
    on.exit(options(old_options), add = TRUE)
    status <- download.file(url, local_file, method = "libcurl", mode = "wb",
                            quiet = TRUE, headers = c("User-Agent" = USER_AGENT))
    if (status != 0) stop("Resource download failed")
    url <- local_file
  }
  data <- read_delim(url, delim = delim, show_col_types = FALSE, ...)
  stop_for_problems(data)
  if (drop_empty_unnamed && nrow(data) > 0) {
    # Blank CSV headers (often from trailing separators) become "...n".
    unnamed <- grepl("^\\.\\.\\.[0-9]+$", names(data))
    empty_unnamed <- unnamed & map_lgl(data, ~ all(is.na(.x)))
    if (any(empty_unnamed)) {
      message("Removed empty unnamed columns: ", paste(names(data)[empty_unnamed], collapse = ", "))
      data <- data[, !empty_unnamed, drop = FALSE]
    }
  }
  data
}
```

## Missing values

```{r missing-values}
missing <- tibble(
  column = names(df),
  missing = map_int(df, ~ sum(is.na(.x))),
  missing_pct = map_dbl(df, ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100)
) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_pct))
missing

# Show up to 20 columns with missing values; percentages use all rows.
missing_plot <- missing |> filter(missing > 0) |> slice_head(n = 20)
if (nrow(missing_plot) > 0) {
  ggplot(missing_plot, aes(x = missing_pct, y = reorder(column, missing_pct))) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
    labs(x = "Missing values (%)", y = NULL, title = "Missingness by column")
} else {
  message("No missing values to plot (or the dataset has no rows).")
}
```

```{r histograms}
# Plot up to four numeric columns, excluding non-finite values only from plots.
numeric_names <- names(select(df, where(is.numeric))) |> head(4)
for (column in numeric_names) {
  values <- df[[column]]
  values <- values[is.finite(values)]
  if (length(values) > 0) {
    plot <- ggplot(tibble(value = values), aes(x = value)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
      labs(title = column, x = column, y = "Count")
    print(plot)
  }
}
```

```{r category-counts}
# Top 10 values for up to three categorical columns, including missing values.
categorical_names <- df |>

  names() |>
  head(3)
for (column in categorical_names) {
  cat(column, "\n")
  df |> count(.data[[column]], sort = TRUE) |> head(10) |> print()
}
```
